## Question 3. RationalQuantity and the sign-refined types

### The designs

- **The advanced chapter**: all rational types are type aliases of one trait,
  `RationalQuantity[\unit U absorbs unit, bool ninf, bool lt, bool eq, bool gt, bool pinf, bool nan\]`
  (numbers-advanced.tex:15-27); eighteen aliases `QQ`, `QQ_LT`, ..., `QQ_splat_NE`
  (:47-66); the trait extends every instantiation of itself with weaker flags,
  `RationalQuantity[\U, ninf', ...\] where { bool ninf', ..., ninf -> ninf', ... }`, and
  conditionally `Field`, `AbelianGroup`, the order and lattice traits (:261-290);
  it coerces `Identity[\+\]`, `Identity[\DOT\]`, the `Zero`s and `IntegerQuantity`
  (:291-298); its operators compute the result's flags by boolean formulas over the
  arguments' flags (:299-420), one of them ending in the words "needs more work here"
  (:364).
- **The basic chapters**: eighteen rational types (QQ, QQ* and QQ#, each with five sign
  refinements) listed as subtypes of one another and of the real ones (numbers.tex:36-91),
  with "the Fortress type system tracks these types closely through various arithmetic
  operations" (:93-96); the same for the
  integers (basic-integers.tex:28-66, 70-73), `NN` a synonym for `ZZ_GE` (:63-65), and
  `ZZ_GT` a lattice under divisibility (:531-535). `ZZ extends { QQ, ZZ_star, ... }`
  (:195-196).
- **Against them**: the language chapter's "these types are mutually exclusive"
  (types-vals-vars.tex:500-505; types.tick:977-981), and the instantiation rule
  (types.tick:353-372): `QQ_GT` would be several instantiations of `RationalQuantity`.

### 1. The refresher

The positive rationals, the nonnegative ones, the rationals with infinities, and the
rationals with an indefinite 0/0 are nested subsets. A value's sign is a property of the
value; tracking it in the type lets a checker prove `x / y` is defined, or that a GCD
lattice applies. Every such refinement has the same representation as its parent.

### 2. What each path does today, measured

- The team's `ProjectFortress/tests/conditionalExtension.fss` (Sukyoung Ryu, 2007)
  declares `RationalQuantity` exactly and "can be parsed": walk runs it and prints its line,
  because nothing instantiates the trait (Q3ConditionalExtension.walk.txt). The compiled
  checker rejects it: "Cyclic type hierarchy: Type RationalQuantity transitively extends
  itself" (Q3ConditionalExtension.comp.txt).
- Instantiating the design on walk fails twice over: the trait-level `where { lt OR eq OR gt }`
  is an InterpreterBug (Q3RefineWalk.walk.txt); without it, the conditional extends reports
  "Missing type lt'" (Q3RefineCondWalk.walk.txt). The compiled checker gives the same
  cyclic-hierarchy error for the probe (Q3RefineCondWalk.comp.txt). A parser quirk met on
  the way: `Rat[\false,true\]` in a parameter type is a syntax error and `Rat[\false, true\]`
  parses.
- The same refinements spelled with the later chapter's covariant static parameters
  (each sign flag a type argument, `Never` below `May`; Q3Phantom.fss): the compiled
  checker accepts it and rejects zero passed where a positive is asked (Q3PhantomReject.comp.txt),
  but the generated class does not implement the covariant supertype and the run stops with
  IncompatibleClassChangeError (Q3Phantom.comp.txt); walk has no covariance ("Unification
  error", Q3Phantom.walk.txt).
- Type aliases (`type X = ...`) appear nowhere in Library/ or in the team's tests.

### 3. What the specification says, including the same idea under another spelling

Beyond the designs above: the per-type `check_LT`, `check_GT`, ... methods, which throw
CastError (numbers.tex:228-244): the refinement as a run-time check. Contracts,
`requires { ... }` (functions.tex:418-426): the refinement as a precondition. Coercion from a
generic type (types.tick:393-400) with where-clauses (conversions-coercions.tex:157-160,
196-220): the refinement ordering as coercions, not subtyping. The later Types chapter
comments out the whole Type Aliases section, including the parallel example
`type SimpleFloat[\nat e, nat s\] = DetailedFloat[\Unity,e,s,false,false,false,false,true\]`
(types.tick:1011-1036), and offers covariant parameters instead (types.tick:322-339). The
language chapter's mutual exclusion is the spec's own flat reading.

### 4. Where it sits in the numeric tower

The designs are a second axis on top of the widths: refinement by sign and by
infinity/NaN, same representation. Today's library has only the width axis, and nests it.
Route A flattens the width axis; the refinement axis, if kept as subtyping, is a lattice of
eighteen types per base type that the instantiation rule forbids in its
`RationalQuantity` spelling.

### 5. What the library already does in the same family

It has: `QQ` as one trait over `Ratio` and the integers (fsi:373-407; fss:524-610);
`RR64.check` and `check_star`, which return `Maybe[\RR64\]` for "finite" and "not NaN"
(fsi:347-350): the refinement as a run-time check, spelled with Maybe where the spec says
CastError; NN32 and NN64 as separate unsigned representations (fsi:438-463,
FortressBuiltin.fsi:82-108), a representation choice, not a sign refinement; and its own
note of the gap, `denominator(self): ZZ  (* Ideally would be NN *)` (fsi:379). It never
had: `RationalQuantity`, `IntegerQuantity`, any `_LT`/`_GT`/`_star`/`_splat` type, `NN`,
`Identity`/`Zero`, or units in the shipped library. The sign-refined names exist only in
`Library/incomplete/basic/Fortress.Number.fsi:12-107` (`QQ extends { RR, QQ_star,
Field[\QQ,QQ_NE,...\] ... }`, `check_LT` and the rest), and units in its siblings
(Fortress.SIUnits and others), a 2008 move of older files (1d2680d4d) that no build
compiles; `RationalQuantity` is nowhere in Library/, not even there. Java has none of this.

### 6. What the peers do, by family

(Reference documentation; not measured here.) *JVM*: none in Java or Kotlin (Kotlin's
`UInt` is a representation, like NN32); Scala's refined-types library encodes predicates
in types. *Close to the metal*: Ada's `subtype Positive is Integer range 1 .. Integer'Last`
(a subtype checked at run time, the spec's `ZZ_GT` exactly); Rust's `NonZeroU32` (a
separate type, `new` returns an Option, `get` converts back: the library's Maybe-returning
`check`). *Scientific*: none in Julia or Fortran; F#'s units of measure and C++'s
Boost.Units carry the `unit U` axis at compile time and erase it. *Unbounded and research*:
Liquid Haskell and F* carry sign refinements in types, checked by an SMT solver.

### 7. The history in the commits

1a736b627 and 368b33727 (Sukyoung Ryu, 2007-08-14 and 2007-12-14): where-clauses on
extends clauses implemented in the parser, and the conditionalExtension test that parses
the design. 1d2680d4d (2008-03-24): the incomplete Number and units libraries moved to
`Library/incomplete`. 6d53c0fc4 (2009-11-03): the advanced numbers chapter enters the
in-repo spec; unchanged since, and identical in Specification-1.0-frozen. The later Types
chapter (2012) comments out type aliases. `git log --all -S RationalQuantity` finds it only
in the specification, in conditionalExtension.fss and in commented-out code added to
`not_passing_yet` (3e034f13c, 2008-07-03): no commit instantiates it.

### 8. The derivation from Pavol's principles

- *The library's patterns*: the library refines by run-time check (`check`, `check_star`
  with Maybe) and by representation (NN32, NN64); it never refined by type.
- *The spec changes when the wish met reality*: the wish is the advanced chapter; the type
  group's rule forbids its spelling, the compiled checker rejects it, the interpreter cannot
  instantiate it, the spec's own language chapter says the numeric types are mutually
  exclusive, and the designers' later chapter removed type aliases. This is the clearest
  "wish met reality" case of the three.
- *Integers, JVM, hardware*: sign refinements have no JVM counterpart and no hardware
  behaviour; unsigned representations (NN32, NN64) do and already have their own types.
- *microGPT*: no program line uses a refined type, `QQ`, units or `where`; nothing in the
  goal needs them.

### 9. The ways, and what each commits Pavol to

1. **Refinement by run-time check on the flat types** (the library's own `check`/`check_star`;
   the spec's `check_GT` family). The spec keeps the advanced chapter's text verbatim as a
   preserved, superseded design, and rewrites the basic chapters' subtype lists as the
   check methods. Commits Pavol to: Maybe or CastError for the check methods (the library
   and the spec differ), and nothing in either implementation.
2. **Refinement by covariant phantom parameters** (the later chapter's `covariant`,
   Q3Phantom). Keeps static tracking without breaking the instantiation rule. Commits
   Pavol to: covariance in the code generator's class hierarchy and in the interpreter
   (both measured missing), and to formulas for result flags that Fortress cannot compute
   at the type level without the spec's boolean static-parameter arithmetic.
3. **Refinement by coercion between sibling types** (route A's own mechanism). Each
   refined type a sibling with coercions to its coarser ones. *Blocking*: coercion does not
   chain (conversions-coercions.tex:127-130), so the lattice needs a coercion for every pair.
   *How the library gets around it elsewhere*: the compiled prelude lists every pair (`ZZ`
   coerces all four fixed widths, CompilerBuiltin.fsi:103-108). Commits Pavol to eighteen
   types per base and 72 coercions among the eighteen rationals alone (one for each pair in
   which one type's flags are a subset of the other's, numbers-advanced.tex:29-46).
4. **One bool-parameterised trait with a generic coercion under a where-clause**
   (`coerce[\bool lt', ...\](x: RationalQuantity[\..., lt', ...\]) where { lt' -> lt, ... }`).
   *Blocking*: where-clauses unsupported (conversions-coercions.tex:15), and walk cannot
   instantiate a trait with a where-clause (measured). Commits Pavol to where-clauses in the
   checker and both back ends.
5. **The spec as written, the rule relaxed for it.** Excluded by the fixed ground.
6. **Drop the refinements from the standard library chapters**, keep the text as
   history, and leave precondition-style refinement to contracts (`requires`). Commits Pavol
   to a smaller library chapter and no implementation work.

**Reading (mine).** Way 1, with the advanced chapter preserved word for word and marked as
the 1.0-era design the type group's rule and the later Types chapter superseded, and the basic
chapters' subtype lists replaced by the check methods the library already has. Way 2 is the
one that keeps the designers' ambition inside their own later rules, and the probes show
how far the implementations are from it; nothing in the microGPT goal asks for it.

    13	\applabel{spec-changes}
    14

    18	\section{Changes Made by the 2026 Revival to the Working Draft}
    19	\seclabel{revival-changes}
    20	\sloppy
    21	
    22	This section lists the changes made to this working draft by the 2026
    23	revival of the Fortress project (\url{https://github.com/palimondo/fortress}).
    24	The revival works to finish what the designers intended, judged by this
    25	working draft, and changes the text only where a decision it has taken for
    26	the implementation would otherwise leave the text and the implementation in
    27	open disagreement.
    28	Each changed passage carries a box headed
    29	``Revised by the 2026 revival'' that points to its entry here.
    30	
    31	Each entry gives the affected sections, the change, its rationale, its
    32	effect, the original text, and what reversing to the alternative not taken
    33	would require.
    34	The original text is that of the \emph{Working Draft of February 2011},
    35	the unrevised copy of this document kept in the revival's repository under
    36	the directory \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/}, cited by path and line
    37	there.
    38	The directory's name is misleading: its sources are the working draft of
    39	2~February 2011, and only the file \nolinkurl{fortress.1.0.pdf} in it is the
    40	Fortress~1.0 release.
    41	The full reasoning behind every entry, with each original passage and each
    42	new one, is in the revival's decision record,
    43	\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-route-a/decision-record.md}
    44	in the same repository.
    45	
    46	Every change below follows from one decision of the revival, taken on
    47	24~September 2026 and called \emph{route~A}: the compiled type checker keeps
    48	the type group's rule that no type is a subtype of two different
    49	instantiations of one parameterized trait, a rule this working draft never
    50	stated, and the library's numeric types are to be reorganized so that they
    51	satisfy it.
    52	The alternative not taken, \emph{route~C}, is described once, in
    53	\secref{revival-routec}.
    54	
    55	\subsection{Instantiation exclusion}
    56	\seclabel{revival-rule}
    57	
    58	\begin{description}
    59	\item[Affected sections] \secref{trait-types}; \secref{trait-decls}.
    60	\item[Change] A property of the exclusion relation is added:
    61	two instantiations of the same parameterized trait exclude each other
    62	unless every static argument other than an operator argument is the same.
    63	The rule it imposes on declarations is added beside the example of
    64	\TYP{InclusiveMolecule}: a trait or object may not extend two such
    65	instantiations, directly or through its supertraits.
    66	\item[Rationale] Without the rule a value may belong to two instantiations
    67	of one parameterized trait, and code specialised for one of them can be
    68	chosen for a caller that was promised the other; with the rule relaxed, the
    69	compiled implementation accepts such a program and fails at run time.
    70	The type group adopted the rule as \emph{multiple instantiation exclusion}
    71	(Allen, Hilburn, Kilpatrick, Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele, ``Type
    72	Checking Modular Multiple Dispatch with Parametric Polymorphism and
    73	Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011), and the compiled type checker has
    74	enforced it since 2010.
    75	The team's later, unfinished Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) states it in
    76	the two parts used here, under the name \emph{instantiation exclusion}.
    77	Operator arguments do not count: an operator argument only names the
    78	operator a subtrait inherits (\secref{opr-ident}), neither implementation
    79	distinguishes instantiations by it at run time, and the algebra of the
    80	library chapters depends on types that are several instantiations of one
    81	trait differing only in operator arguments.
    82	\KWD{nat}, \KWD{int} and \KWD{bool} arguments count: they are values at
    83	run time (\secref{natparams}, \secref{boolparams}).
    84	\item[Effect] Programs in which a type is a subtype of two instantiations
    85	of one parameterized trait that differ in any other static argument are no
    86	longer valid. The compiled type checker refuses them where the arguments
    87	that differ are types, or numerals given as \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int}
    88	arguments (row~402 of the revival's gap ledger). It does not yet refuse
    89	them where those arguments are \KWD{bool} arguments, though it accepts boolean parameters written out (row~406),
    90	or where one of them is a static parameter of the trait or object that extends both (row~414).
    91	The interpreter does not check the rule.
    92	The library's numeric chapters are not yet revised
    93	(\secref{revival-notrevised}).
    94	\item[Original text] The Working Draft of February 2011 states no such
    95	property; its relations are ``the smallest ones that satisfy all the
    96	properties given in those sections (and this one)''
    97	(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/types-vals-vars.tex}, lines
    98	185--189), and the properties it gives for trait types are these (lines
    99	212--216):
   100	\begin{quote}
   101	A trait declaration may also include an \KWD{excludes} clause,
   102	in which case the defined trait type
   103	excludes every type that appears in that clause.
   104	Every trait type also excludes every arrow type and every tuple type,
   105	and the special types \TYP{()} and \TYP{BottomType}.
   106	\end{quote}
   107	Its rule on declarations is only that of exclusive traits,
   108	``no trait can extend them both''
   109	(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex}, lines 218--222).
   110	\item[Route C] Replaces this rule by the rule of \secref{revival-routec}.
   111	\end{description}
   112	
   113	\subsection{Where-clause variables in extends clauses}
   114	\seclabel{revival-where}
   115	
   116	\begin{description}
   117	\item[Affected sections] \secref{where-clauses}; \secref{trait-decls}.
   118	\item[Change] One sentence is added: a \KWD{where}-clause variable may not
   119	appear as a static argument in an \KWD{extends} clause.
   120	The three declarations that followed it are kept, marked
   121	``Not allowed'', each with the way to write it
   122	(\secref{revival-covariance}, \secref{revival-every},
   123	\secref{revival-empty}).
   124	A box after Victor Luchangco's two draft notes in \secref{trait-decls},
   125	which say that a trait can explicitly extend itself through hidden type
   126	variables and that ``we could just rule this a special case'', answers
   127	them.
   128	\item[Rationale] Such a variable makes the declared type a subtype of one
   129	instantiation for each type the variable may stand for, and instantiation
   130	exclusion forbids any two of them.
   131	\item[Effect] None of the three declarations ran before the revision:
   132	both implementations stop at name resolution, because a
   133	\KWD{where}-clause variable is not in scope in an \KWD{extends} clause.
   134	The revision makes that the rule.
   135	The calculus of \appref{where-calculus} still admits such
   136	declarations (\secref{revival-calculi}).
   137	\item[Original text] No such sentence; the draft notes are unchanged.
   138	\item[Route C] The same under route~C, which places no type below
   139	infinitely many instantiations of one trait.
   140	\end{description}

   142	\subsection{The covariance example}
   143	\seclabel{revival-covariance}
   144	
   145	\begin{description}
   146	\item[Affected section] \secref{where-clauses}.
   147	\item[Change] The declaration is kept, marked ``Not allowed''; the claims
   148	that trait declarations may extend other instantiations of themselves and
   149	that the declaration expresses covariance are withdrawn; static
   150	parameters are stated to be invariant, and a widening function with
   151	bounded static parameters is given as the way to convert one
   152	instantiation to another.
   153	\item[Rationale] \EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket} would be a subtype of
   154	\EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} for every supertype \VAR{T} of \VAR{S}.
   155	The widening function is how the library writes covariance, in the
   156	conversions and the \OPR{APPCOV} operator of its covariant collections,
   157	and it runs on both implementations.
   158	\item[Effect] Covariance is written as an explicit conversion, with the
   159	static arguments given at the call. The box at the example adds that the
   160	type group's later design declares variance with a \KWD{covariant}
   161	modifier, implemented on neither implementation; the decision record and
   162	row~404 of the revival's gap ledger say what is known of it.
   163	\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/trait-parameters.tex},

   165	``Not allowed'', and the text around it read:
   166	\begin{quote}
   167	Trait declarations are allowed to extend other instantiations of
   168	themselves. For example, we can write:
   169	[the declaration]
   170	In this declaration, for every subtype \VAR{S} of \VAR{T}, \EXP{C\llbracket{}S\rrbracket}
   171	is a subtype of \EXP{C\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}. Effectively, we have expressed
   172	  the fact that the static parameter \VAR{S} of \VAR{C} is covariant.
   173	\end{quote}

   177	\subsection{A subtrait of every instantiation}
   178	\seclabel{revival-every}
   179	
   180	\begin{description}
   181	\item[Affected section] \secref{where-clauses}.
   182	\item[Change] ``the following trait declaration is legal'' becomes
   183	``is not allowed''; the paragraph after the declaration is kept, in the
   184	conditional, and a closing sentence says why the declaration is not
   185	allowed.
   186	\item[Rationale] The paragraph is the team's own account of why such a
   187	trait is dangerous, written before the rule; it becomes the reason for the
   188	rule.
   189	\item[Effect] None beyond \secref{revival-where}.
   190	\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/trait-parameters.tex},
   191	lines 354--380; the declaration is the one kept above, and the text around
   192	it read:
   193	\begin{quote}
   194	Trait declarations need not have any static parameters in order
   195	to have a \KWD{where} clause. For example, the following trait
   196	declaration is legal:
   197	[the declaration]
   198	In this declaration, trait \VAR{C} is a subtrait of \emph{every}
   199	instantiation of parametric trait \VAR{D}. Thus, trait \VAR{C} has all
   200	of the methods of every instantiation of \VAR{D}. By thinking of the
   201	declaration this way, we can see what restrictions we need to impose on
   202	the trait \VAR{C} in order for it to be sensible. [The rest of the
   203	paragraph is unchanged.]
   204	\end{quote}
   205	\item[Route C] The same under route~C.

   208	\subsection{The empty list}
   209	\seclabel{revival-empty}
   210	
   211	\begin{description}
   212	\item[Affected section] \secref{where-clauses}.
   213	\item[Change] The declaration of \TYP{Empty} is kept, marked
   214	``Not allowed''; \EXP{\TYP{Empty}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}, one empty list
   215	for each element type, is given beside it.
   216	\item[Rationale] The original makes \TYP{Empty} a
   217	\EXP{\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} for every \VAR{T} at once.
   218	The replacement is the library's own shape for its empty collections and
   219	the same choice as for \TYP{Nothing} (\secref{revival-nothing}); a program
   220	of this shape runs on both implementations.
   221	\item[Effect] The element type is written at each use, as in
   222	\EXP{\TYP{Empty}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket}, until the static
   223	arguments of a generic object can be inferred, which neither
   224	implementation does today. The section no longer has a running example of
   225	a \KWD{where} clause on an object.
   226	\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/trait-parameters.tex},
   227	lines 383--399; the declaration is the one kept above, introduced by:
   228	\begin{quote}
   229	Object or functional declarations may include \KWD{where} clauses.
   230	Here is an example declaration of an \TYP{Empty} list:
   231	\end{quote}
   232	\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
   233	\end{description}

   235	\subsection{The empty optional value}
   236	\seclabel{revival-nothing}
   237	
   238	\begin{description}
   239	\item[Affected sections] \secref{convenience-types};
   240	\secref{chained-exceptions}; \chapref{lib:exception}.
   241	\item[Change] \TYP{Nothing} becomes
   242	\EXP{\KWD{value}\;\;\KWD{object}\:\TYP{Nothing}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
   243	extending \EXP{\TYP{Maybe}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}, with no
   244	\KWD{excludes} clause, and \TYP{Maybe} comprises
   245	\EXP{\TYP{Nothing}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} and
   246	\EXP{\TYP{Just}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}; the original declaration is kept,
   247	marked ``Not allowed''. The defaults of an exception's message and chain
   248	become \EXP{\TYP{Nothing}\llbracket\TYP{String}\rrbracket} and
   249	\EXP{\TYP{Nothing}\llbracket\TYP{Exception}\rrbracket}.
   250	\item[Rationale] The original makes \TYP{Nothing} a
   251	\EXP{\TYP{Maybe}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} for every \VAR{T} at once. Its
   252	\KWD{excludes} clause is also one the grammar gives no object declaration
   253	(\secref{object-decls}), and is redundant, an object trait type already
   254	excluding every type that is not its supertype (\secref{object-traits}).
   255	The replacement is the library's declaration.
   256	\item[Effect] The empty case is written with its type, as in
   257	\EXP{\TYP{Nothing}\llbracket\TYP{String}\rrbracket}, until the static
   258	arguments of a generic object can be inferred from the type expected.
   259	The compiled path's own library, used until the one library replaces it,
   260	still declares a single \TYP{Nothing} with a coercion to every
   261	\EXP{\TYP{Maybe}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}, and refuses
   262	\EXP{\TYP{Nothing}\llbracket\TYP{String}\rrbracket}
   263	(row~331 of the revival's gap ledger).
   264	\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/convenience.tex},
   265	lines 34--53: the declaration kept above, marked ``Not allowed'', together
   266	with:
   267	\begin{quote}
   268	An optional value \VAR{v} is either \TYP{Nothing} or
   269	\EXP{\TYP{Just}(v)} declared as follows:
   270	[\ldots]
   271	\begin{Fortress}
   272	\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Maybe}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket \KWD{comprises} \{\,\TYP{Nothing}, \TYP{Just}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket\,\}\)
   273	\end{Fortress}
   274	[\ldots]
   275	\end{quote}
   276	\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/exceptions.tex}, lines 111--130:
   277	\begin{quote}
   278	These fields are default to \TYP{Nothing} as follows: [\ldots]
   279	\begin{Fortress}
   280	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{getter} \VAR{message}()\COLON \TYP{Maybe}\llbracket\TYP{String}\rrbracket = \TYP{Nothing}\)\\
   281	\(  \ldots\)\\
   282	\(  \KWD{getter} \VAR{chain}()\COLON \TYP{Maybe}\llbracket\TYP{Exception}\rrbracket = \TYP{Nothing}\)\-\\\poptabs
   283	\end{Fortress}
   284	[\ldots]
   285	where an optional value \VAR{v} is either \TYP{Nothing} or
   286	\EXP{\TYP{Just}(v)}.
   287	\end{quote}
   288	\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/exception.tex}, lines 22--24:
   289	\begin{quote}
   290	These fields are default to \TYP{Nothing}
   291	where an optional value \VAR{v} is either \TYP{Nothing} or
   292	\EXP{\TYP{Just}(v)} as declared in \secref{convenience-types}.
   293	\end{quote}
   294	\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
   295	\end{description}

   297	\subsection{The root's algebra}
   298	\seclabel{revival-object}
   299	
   300	\begin{description}
   301	\item[Affected sections] \chapref{lib:object}.
   302	\item[Change] \TYP{Object} extends \TYP{Any} alone and \TYP{Tuple} likewise,
   303	each still excluding the other; the sentences saying that they describe
   304	their operators with algebraic constraints are removed. The original
   305	declaration of \TYP{Object} is kept, marked ``Not allowed''.
   306	\item[Rationale] Every trait but \TYP{Any} and \TYP{Object} extends
   307	\TYP{Object}, and every commutative algebraic type \VAR{T} is an
   308	\EXP{\TYP{EquivalenceRelation}\llbracket{}T,=\rrbracket}; with the
   309	original declaration such a type is also an
   310	\EXP{\TYP{EquivalenceRelation}\llbracket\TYP{Object},\sequiv\rrbracket},
   311	and the two differ in a type argument. \TYP{Tuple}'s declaration is not
   312	refused by the rule, since no tuple type extends a trait, but its text
   313	follows \TYP{Object}'s. The replacement is the library's declaration.
   314	\item[Effect] The properties of \EXP{\sequiv} are those stated in trait
   315	\TYP{Any}; they are no longer restated at \TYP{Object} through the
   316	algebra chapter.
   317	\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/objects.tex}
   318	(whose lines are two fewer than this document's source), line 82:
   319	\begin{quote}
   320	In \TYP{Object} this property is asserted abstractly using the algebraic constraints of \chapref{lib:algebraic-constraints}.
   321	\end{quote}
   322	lines 125--139, the declaration kept above, marked ``Not allowed'', after:
   323	\begin{quote}
   324	The \TYP{Object} type does not
   325	have any additional methods, but uses algebraic constraints (see
   326	\chapref{lib:algebraic-constraints}) to describe the properties of the
   327	existing operators more abstractly.
   328	\end{quote}
   329	and lines 145--156:
   330	\begin{quote}
   331	As with the type \TYP{Object}, the type \TYP{Tuple} uses algebraic constraints to describe its existing methods.
   332	\begin{Fortress}
   333	\(\KWD{trait}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu\TYP{Tuple} \KWD{extends} \{\,\TYP{Any}, \TYP{EquivalenceRelation}\llbracket\TYP{Tuple},\sequiv\rrbracket, \TYP{IdentityOperator}\llbracket\TYP{Tuple}\rrbracket\,\}\)\\
   334	{\tt~~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \KWD{excludes} \{\,\TYP{Object}\,\}\)\-\\\poptabs
   335	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{toString}()\COLON \TYP{String}\)\-\\\poptabs
   336	\(\KWD{end}\)
   337	\end{Fortress}
   338	\end{quote}
   339	\item[Route C] By the revival's reading, not measured, the original
   340	declaration of \TYP{Object} is one of the two passages that would read
   341	differently under route~C, the numeric chapters being the other.
   342	\end{description}
   343	
   344	\subsection{The internal document}
   345	\seclabel{revival-internal}
   346	
   347	\begin{description}
   348	\item[Affected sections] In the appendix ``Internal Document'', which
   349	follows this one in a draft build: ``Disjunctive Constraints'',
   350	``Weirdness with Multiple Inheritance and Polymorphism'' and
   351	``Conditional Subtyping''.
   352	\item[Change] One box after each: the first program's premise is not
   353	allowed; the second is the case the rule answers; the third declaration is
   354	not allowed for the reason the covariance example is not.
   355	\item[Rationale] Instantiation exclusion.
   356	\item[Effect] None; the internal document is printed only in a draft
   357	build.
   358	\item[Original text] Unchanged.
   359	\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
   360	\end{description}
   361	
   362	\subsection{The calculi}
   363	\seclabel{revival-calculi}
   364	
   365	\begin{description}
   366	\item[Affected sections] In \appref{calculi}: \basiccore\
   367	(Section~\ref{basic-calculus}), \wherecore\ (\appref{where-calculus}),
   368	\overloadingcore\ (\appref{overloading-calculus}) and \acffdcore\
   369	(Section~\ref{acffd-calculus}).
   370	\item[Change] One box at the opening of each calculus, saying that the
   371	calculus predates instantiation exclusion and naming the shape it admits
   372	that the rule refuses: in \basiccore, an object that extends two different
   373	instantiations of a parameterized trait declaring no method, so that its
   374	statement that all of its valid programs are valid Fortress programs no
   375	longer holds for every program; in \wherecore, a \KWD{where}-clause
   376	variable in a supertype, which its subtyping rule turns into one supertype
   377	for each witness of the variable; in \overloadingcore, the same object as
   378	in \basiccore, which its rule for valid method declarations admits because
   379	the trait declares no method; in \acffdcore, a trait that extends an
   380	instantiation of itself at its parameter's bound, which conditions (2)
   381	and (3) of its rule for an acyclic type hierarchy admit.
   382	The rules of the calculi and their soundness claims are not changed.
   383	\item[Rationale] The calculi are the team's formal record of this working
   384	draft as it stood, and the rule changes the language, not that record.
   385	New premises in their rules would be new formal work, and would reopen
   386	soundness claims that were proved for the rules as they are written.
   387	The revival decided on this treatment on 26~September 2026.
   388	\item[Effect] None on the language or on either implementation.
   389	The four calculi admit programs, in the shapes named, that are not valid
   390	Fortress programs.
   391	\item[Original text] The calculi are unchanged. The statement that the box
   392	in \basiccore\ qualifies is in
   393	\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/calculi/basic/calculus.tex},
   394	lines 16--19:
   395	\begin{quote}
   396	Following the precedent set by prior core calculi such as Featherweight
   397	Generic Java~\cite{fgj},
   398	we have abided by the restriction that all valid \basiccore\ programs are
   399	valid Fortress programs.
   400	\end{quote}
   401	The shapes the other three boxes name are admitted by
   402	\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/calculi/where/syntax.tex},
   403	lines 82--91, and
   404	\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/calculi/where/static.tex},
   405	lines 53--81 and 329--342, by
   406	\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/calculi/overloading/static.tex},
   407	lines 52--82, 107--136 and 270--275, and by
   408	\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/calculi/acffd/static.tex},
   409	lines 46--88.
   410	Before this entry, \secref{revival-notrevised} said of the calculi:
   411	\begin{quote}
   412	The calculi of \appref{calculi} predate the rule and are not yet revised:
   413	the calculus with \KWD{where} clauses (\appref{where-calculus}) lets a
   414	\KWD{where}-clause variable occur in a supertype, the calculus with an
   415	acyclic type hierarchy admits a trait that extends an instantiation of
   416	itself at its parameter's bound, and the basic calculus states that all of
   417	its valid programs are valid Fortress programs, while it admits an object
   418	that extends two instantiations of a parameterized trait declaring no
   419	method.
   420	How they are to be revised awaits a decision of the revival.
   421	\end{quote}
   422	That paragraph did not name \overloadingcore, whose box was added after
   423	the other three.
   424	\item[Route C] By the revival's reading, not measured, the same under
   425	route~C: none of the shapes named is a chain of instantiations of a
   426	self-typed parameterized trait, the one case route~C relaxes.
   427	\end{description}
   428	
   429	\subsection{Passages not yet revised}
   430	\seclabel{revival-notrevised}
   431	
   432	The number chapters, \chapref{lib:numbers-basic} (whose integers are \secref{basic-integers})
   433	and \chapref{lib:numbers-advanced}, are not yet revised.
   434	Their nested tower, in which each integer type is a subtype of the rational
   435	one above it and each carries its algebra at its own type, and the
   436	conditional self-extension of \TYP{RationalQuantity}, are refused by
   437	instantiation exclusion, as the compiled type checker refuses the
   438	library's nested tower today.
   439	They will be revised together with the reorganization of the library's
   440	numeric types that route~A decides, and not before, because a
   441	specification ahead of its library is as much an open discrepancy as one
   442	behind it.
   443	Until then the rule refuses the tower these chapters describe.
   444	
   445	\subsection{Route C, the alternative not taken}
   446	\seclabel{revival-routec}
   447	
   448	The team's 2012 patent applications (US~8,843,887 and US~8,898,632;
   449	Chase, Steele, Naden, Hilburn, and Luchangco) relax the rule for a
   450	self-typed parameterized trait: a type may be a subtype of several of its
   451	instantiations when they form a chain.
   452	The revival built that rule whole as an experiment and measured it.
   453	It closes the unsoundness that instantiation exclusion guards against only
   454	together with a rule on return types over every level of a chain and a
   455	change in how a call chooses among generic methods specialised to
   456	different instantiations: 188 lines of code in five files of the compiled
   457	type checker and code generator.
   458	Reversing route~A for route~C would also need a method per level of a
   459	chain in the code generator, work in the interpreter, a way past a stack
   460	overflow of the type checker on the self-typing clauses, and seven library
   461	declarations, besides undoing the reorganization of the library's numeric
   462	types.
   463	Route~C rescues none of the \KWD{where}-clause examples of
   464	\secref{where-clauses} nor the \TYP{Nothing} of \secref{convenience-types},
   465	each of which places one type below infinitely many instantiations, which
   466	no chain contains.
   467	Under route~C the numeric chapters could keep their nested tower, and the
   468	original text of those chapters, kept unrevised in this document for now
   469	and in the Working Draft of February 2011, is route~C's.
   470	The record of the experiment is
   471	\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/mie-probes/route-c-experiment.md} in the
   472	revival's repository.
   473	\fussy

     6	%   Use is subject to license terms.
     7	%
     8	%   This distribution may include materials developed by third parties.
     9	%
    10	%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
    11	
    12	\section{Summations and Other Reduction Expressions}
    13	\seclabel{reduction-expr}
    14	
    15	\begin{Grammar}
    16	\emph{FlowExpr} &::=&
    17	\emph{Accumulator} \option{\emph{StaticArgs}}
    18	\options{\texttt[ \emph{GeneratorClauseList} \texttt]} \emph{Expr} \\
    19	
    20	\emph{Accumulator} &::=& $\sum$ $|$ $\prod$ $|$ \KWD{BIG} (\emph{Encloser} $|$ \emph{Op})
    21	\end{Grammar}
    22	
    23	A \emph{reduction expression} begins with a big operator such as
    24	$\sum$ or $\prod$ followed by an optional static arguments and
    25	an optional generator clause list (described in
    26	\secref{generators}), followed by a body expression.
    27	There is no explicit relationship between \EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\emph{Op}} and
    28	\emph{Op}.  Instead, a reduction expression corresponds to a call to the
    29	\EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\emph{Op}} operator, which has the following header:
    30	%% opr BIG Op[\T\](g:(Reduction[\R0\],T->R0)->R0):R
    31	\begin{Fortress}
    32	\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{BIG}}\: \emph{Op}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(g\COLONOP(\TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket,T\rightarrow{}R_{0})\rightarrow{}R_{0})\COLONOP{}R\)
    33	\end{Fortress}
    34	Here \VAR{R} is the result type of the operator, and \VAR{g} corresponds to
    35	the method %generate[\R0\]
    36	\EXP{\VAR{generate}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket}
    37	of the trait %Generator[\T\]
    38	\EXP{\TYP{Generator}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}:
    39	it is a function that takes a reduction (of type %Reduction[\R0\]
    40	\EXP{\TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket})
    41	and a body (of type \EXP{T\rightarrow{}R_{0}})
    42	and returns a value of type \EXP{R_{0}} by running body on each
    43	generated element and combining them using the reduction.
    44	When a generator clause
    45	list is provided, generator clauses produce values and bind the values to the
    46	identifiers that are used in the subexpression.  Each iteration of the
    47	body expression is assumed to be evaluated in a separate implicit
    48	thread as described in \secref{generators}.  The resulting values are
    49	combined together using \emph{Op}
    50	\label{redexpr-redvar}
    51	as with reduction variables (see \secref{reduction-vars}).
    52	The value of a reduction expression is this combined value.
    53	When no generator clause list is provided, the body is taken to be an
    54	object of type \TYP{Generator} and the elements it generates are
    55	combined.  Thus, the reduction expression \EXP{\sum a} is equivalent
    56	to \EXP{\sum\limits_{x\leftarrow{}a}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu{x}}.
    57	
    58	A reduction expression with a generator list:
    59	%% \sum [v_1 \gets g_1, v_2 \gets g_2, \ldots] e
    60	\begin{Fortress}
    61	\(\sum [v_{\mathrm{1}} \gets g_{\mathrm{1}}, v_{\mathrm{2}} \gets g_{\mathrm{2}}, \ldots] e\)
    62	\end{Fortress}
    63	is equivalent to the following code:
    64	%do
    65	%  var result: ZZ32 = 0
    66	%  for v1 <- g1, v2 <- g2, \ldots do
    67	%    result += e
    68	%  end
    69	%  result
    70	%end
    71	\begin{Fortress}
    72	\(\KWD{do}\)\\
    73	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{var}\:\VAR{result}\COLON \mathbb{Z}32 = 0\)\\
    74	\(  \KWD{for}\:v_{1} \leftarrow g_{1}, v_{2} \leftarrow g_{2}, \ldots \KWD{do}\)\\
    75	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \VAR{result} \mathrel{+}= e\)\-\\\poptabs
    76	\(  \KWD{end}\)\\
    77	\(  \VAR{result}\)\-\\\poptabs
    78	\(\KWD{end}\)
    79	\end{Fortress}
    80	where \VAR{result} is a fresh variable.
    81	%
    82	A reduction expression without a generator clause list:
    83	%% \sum g
    84	\begin{Fortress}
    85	\(\sum g\)
    86	\end{Fortress}
    87	is equivalent to the following:
    88	%\sum [x \gets g] x
    89	\begin{Fortress}
    90	\(\sum [x \gets g] x\)
    91	\end{Fortress}
    92	Note that reduction expressions without generator clause lists can be used to
    93	conveniently sum any aggregate expression (described in
    94	\secref{aggregate-expr}), since every aggregate expression
    95	is a generator.
    96	
    97	\section{Parallel Prefix and Parallel Suffix}
    98	\note{This section was not in F1.0$\beta$ nor in F1.0.  We don't quite have a story on this yet.}

490	A function type is a subtype of each of its constituent arrow types,
   491	and also of \TYP{Any}.
   492	Like object trait types and object expression types,
   493	a function type excludes every type that is not its supertype.
   494	
   495	
   496	\section{Special Types}
   497	\seclabel{bottom-type}
   498	
   499	Fortress provides three special types: \TYP{Any}, \TYP{BottomType} and \TYP{()}.
   500	The type \TYP{Any} is the top of the type hierarchy:
   501	it is a supertype of every type.
   502	The only type it excludes is \TYP{BottomType}.
   503	
   504	The type \TYP{()} is the type of the value \EXP{()}.
   505	Its only supertype (other than itself) is \TYP{Any},
   506	and it excludes every other type.
   507	
   508	Fortress provides a special \emph{bottom type}, \TYP{BottomType},
   509	which is an uninhabited type.

# The flattening rung's three questions, and every way to answer them

Route A is fixed ground: the interpreter's library becomes the one library the compiled
checker accepts; the checker keeps the rule that no type is two different instantiations
of one generic ("multiple instantiation exclusion", Papers/Types/introduction.tick:417-426;
types.tick:353-372); so the fixed-width integers, ZZ, QQ and RR64 become siblings under
Number, Number loses its catch-all operators, and each wider type gets a `coerce` from the
narrower one. This note does not decide. It lists, for each of the three questions the rung
meets, the ways the language, the specification, the library and the two implementations
offer, the library's own way first, each taken through the nine steps of protocol § 6.
Readings marked as mine close each part.

**Terms.** *Walk*: the interpreter, `bin/fortress X.fss`, with FortressLibrary.
*Compiled path*: `bin/fortress compile` and run, which today uses the compiler's own
prelude (CompilerBuiltin, CompilerLibrary; Shell.java:403-407 switches to it). *The
checker over the library*: the compiled phase order with FortressLibrary in scope, the
checker-count tool's driver (explorations/coordinator/tools/checker-count/WorldFlip.java).
*Catch-all*: an operator or function declared on `Number` that takes any number and
answers by converting both sides to a float (FortressLibrary.fss:374-422, every body is
`asFloat(self) op asFloat(b)`). *Coercion*: an implicit conversion declared in the target
type (`coerce(x: T)`), applied where a declared type is expected
(conversions-coercions.tex:85-110). *Widening*: the specification's "widest-need"
re-choice of an operator so that a narrow computation is done in the wide type its context
needs (conversions-coercions.tex:762-906). *Identity*: the value `z` with `z + x = x`; the
sum of nothing.

**Probes.** Every probe and its capture is in `flattening-questions-ways/`: `walk.sh`,
`comp.sh` (with `libcache.sh`, which compiles the compiler prelude into a private cache
first) and `check.sh` run one probe in a private cache and write `<Probe>.walk.txt`,
`.comp.txt` or `.check.txt`. The two `Q3ConditionalExtension.*.txt` captures ran the
team's own `ProjectFortress/tests/conditionalExtension.fss` the same way from its
directory, and `Q0FlatArraysComp.comp.txt` is the head and tail of compiling
`explorations/run-c4/src/FlatArrays.fss` on the compiled path. Machine: 4 cores,
Intel Xeon 2.10GHz, JDK 25, `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`; no timings were taken.

**One premise of the brief, corrected by the history.** The compiler prelude was not
flattened by Guy Steele in 2011. David Chase cut the subtyping on 2009-08-31 ("ZZ32 is NOT
a subtype of ZZ64, RR32 is NOT a subtype of RR64; this would be a good time to get
coercion working", 6896886fb); Sukyoung Ryu added the exclusions (3e0306166, 2009-10-16);
Jan-Willem Maessen with Eric Allen, Justin Hilburn and Scott Kilpatrick made ZZ32 coerce
IntLiteral "as described in the spec ... as we gradually migrate to a flat numeric
hierarchy" (128f313b5, 2009-11-17); Eric Allen added ZZ64's coercions from IntLiteral and
ZZ32 and RR64's from RR32 and FloatLiteral (2ef730c88, d0cde7d17, 2010-01); Steele then
built on the flat prelude: the ZZ32 and ZZ64 operators (da5291587, 2011-07-22), the ZZ32
big + and big MAX (d535963cb, 2011-10-12), and ZZ's coercions from all four fixed widths
(304f2743a, 2012-06-12).

---

12	\chapter{Conversions and Coercions}
    13	\chaplabel{conversions-coercions}
    14	
    15	\note{Widening and where clauses are not yet supported.
    16	
    17	The examples in this chapter are not tested nor run by the interpreter.}
    18	
    19	\note{
    20	\begin{itemize}
    21	 \item ``has a type'' vs ``is a subtype of the type or could be coerced to the type''
    22	\item Coercion between tuple types (Victor's email titled ``Coercion between tuple types'' on 07/16/07) and arrow types
    23	
    24	\item Vectors and matrices: \secref{aggregate-expr}
    25	
    26	\item Do we allow coercion declarations in object expressions?
    27	
    28	\item If tests and coercion
    29	
    30	Suppose a test in an expression has a type that is not \TYP{Boolean}
    31	(or a subtype of \TYP{Boolean}) but is coercible to \TYP{Boolean}.
    32	Presumably, that is not a static error? But note that F1.0 beta
    33	makes no mention of this case; all tests in an if expression must be of
    34	type \TYP{Boolean}. There are similar problems with other expression types;
    35	we need to revisit them all in light of the coercion facility...
    36	
    37	\end{itemize}
    38	}
    39	
    40	Fortress provides a mechanism, called \emph{coercion}, to allow a
    41	value of one type to be automatically converted to a value of another
    42	type.  Programmers can define coercions (described in
    43	\secref{coercion-declarations}) and coercions may change the set of
    44	applicable declarations for a call (as described in
    45	\secref{applicability-with-coercion}).  If multiple coercions can be
    46	applied to a particular functional call then the most appropriate
    47	coercion is chosen statically.  Restrictions on coercion declarations
    48	(described in \secref{restrictions-coercion}) guarantee that the
    49	static resolution of coercion (described in
    50	\secref{resolving-coercion}) is well-defined.  Fortress provides
    51	implicit coercions for tuple types and arrow types (described in
    52	\secref{coercion-tuple-arrow}).  Fortress also provides an additional
    53	feature of coercion that allows ``widest-need'' evaluation of
    54	numerical expressions (described in \secref{widening}).
    55	
    56	\section{Principles of Coercion}
    57	\seclabel{coercion}
    58	
    59	In certain situations it is convenient to be able to use a value of
    60	one type \VAR{T} as if it were a value of another type \VAR{U} even
    61	though \VAR{T} is not a subtype of \VAR{U}.  For example, it is
    62	convenient to be able to use an integer-valued expression
    63	in a floating-point expression even though its
    64	type is not a subtype of any floating-point type.  Fortress supports
    65	the automatic conversion of integer values to floating-point values (the
    66	technical term for this kind of automatic conversion is coercion).  In
    67	this way one can write \EXP{(x + 1)/2} rather than \EXP{(x +
    68	1.0)/2.0}, for example.  Such coercion applies generally to function
    69	and method (collectively called as functional) calls as well as to
    70	operators; one can write \EXP{\ln 2} rather than \EXP{\ln 2.0}, or
    71	\EXP{\arctan(1,1)} rather than \EXP{\arctan(1.0,1.0)}, for example.
    72	
    73	One way to think about coercion is that if type \VAR{T} can be coerced
    74	to type \VAR{U}, then a value of type \VAR{T} can be used to ``stand
    75	in'' for a value of type \VAR{U} in a functional call, for example.  This is
    76	different from actually \emph{being} of type \VAR{U}; it means only
    77	that, given any value of type \VAR{T}, an appropriate value of type
    78	\VAR{U} can be computed to substitute for it.  Also, coercion occurs
    79	only when the declared type of the corresponding parameter in the
    80	functional declaration is exactly the type \VAR{U} being coerced to
    81	 not if it is a supertype of \VAR{U}.  Note, however, that if type
    82	 \VAR{T} can be coerced to type \VAR{U} then any subtype of \VAR{T}
    83	 can also be coerced to type \VAR{U}.
    84	
    85	Coercion from \VAR{T} to \VAR{U} may occur in an expression context
    86	where the context expects the expression to have type \VAR{U} and
    87	the type of the expression is a subtype of \VAR{T} except for the following
    88	cases:
    89	\begin{itemize}
    90	\item type ascriptions (see \secref{type-ascription})
    91	\item type assumptions (see \secref{type-assumption})
    92	\end{itemize}
    93	For example, a coercion may occur in a variable definition when the
    94	declared type of the variable is \VAR{U} and the type of the expression on
    95	the right-hand side is a subtype of \VAR{T}.
    96	
    97	
    98	The expression contexts where a coercion can occur are:
    99	\begin{itemize}
   100	\item the right-hand sides of variable and field declarations where the
   101	  left-hand sides have declared types
   102	\item arguments to functionals and constructors where the corresponding
   103	  parameters have declared types
   104	\item body expressions of functionals and constructors where the return
   105	  types are declared
   106	\item the right-hand sides of test and property declarations
   107	\item expressions in contracts
   108	\item expressions whose enclosing expressions constrain the types of
   109	  their subexpressions
   110	\end{itemize}
   111	\chapref{expressions} describes the type constraints for each expression in
   112	Fortress.
   113	
   114	\note{
   115	  \begin{itemize}
   116	\item assignment expressions with type on the left-hand sides
   117	\item filter in a generator
   118	\item spawn
   119	\item throw
   120	\item while Expr
   121	\item if Expr
   122	\item if . then Expr end
   123	\item at Expr
   124	  \end{itemize}
   125	}
   126	
   127	Coercion is \emph{not} automatically chained in Fortress, unlike some
   128	other programming languages: even if type \VAR{T} can be coerced to
   129	type \VAR{U} and type \VAR{U} can be coerced to type \VAR{V}, it is
   130	not necessarily the case that type \VAR{T} can be coerced to type
   131	\VAR{V}.  Type \VAR{T} can be coerced to type \VAR{V} only if this
   132	coercion is explicitly defined.
   133	
   134	The basic principles behind coercion are (1) a decision by the
   135	designer of a trait \VAR{U} that, in all circumstances where a
   136	functional is to be called, an actual argument of some other type
   137	\VAR{T} may be used to satisfy a parameter of type
   138	\VAR{T}, and (2) a language mechanism for putting this decision into
   139	effect automatically and concisely.

   531	\chapref{overloaded-declarations} guarantee that such a $T$
   532	exists and that it is unique.  The call $\f(\As)$ or $\As_0.\f(\As)$ is
   533	rewritten to \EXP{f(\mathrm{coercion}\llbracket{T}\rrbracket(\TYP{A}))} or
   534	\EXP{A_{0}.f(\mathrm{coerce}\llbracket{T}\rrbracket(A))}
   535	and the declaration with parameter
   536	type $T$ is applied to the call.
   537	
   538	As an example, consider the following definitions:
   539	%trait ZZ32 end
   540	%trait ZZ64
   541	%  coerce(z:ZZ32) = ...
   542	%end
   543	%trait ZZ128
   544	%  coerce(z:ZZ32) = ...
   545	%  coerce(z:ZZ64) = ...
   546	%end
   547	%
   548	%f(z:ZZ64) = 1
   549	%f(z:ZZ128) = 2
   550	\begin{Fortress}
   551	\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}32 \KWD{end}\)\\
   552	\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}64\)\\
   553	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}32) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
   554	\(\KWD{end}\)\\
   555	\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z}128\)\\
   556	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}32) = \ldots\)\\
   557	\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
   558	\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
   559	\(f(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}64) = 1\)\\
   560	\(f(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}128) = 2\)
   561	\end{Fortress}
   562	Then the call \EXP{f(\mathbb{Z}32)} resolves to the
   563	declaration \EXP{f(\mathbb{Z}64)} because $\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
   564	\morespecific \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}$, which follows from the fact that
   565	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} coerces to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}128}.
   566	
   567	Notice that coercion is resolved statically.  Once a coercion is
   568	statically chosen for a call, this coercion is conceptually inserted
   569	into the call.
   570	This means that the statically chosen coercion is applied at run time.
   571	
   572	For example, in the following program:
   573	%trait A
   574	%  coerce(c:C) = ...
   575	%end
   576	%trait B excludes A end
   577	%trait C end
   578	%object D extends {B,C} end
   579	%
   580	%f(a:A) = 3
   581	%f(b:B) = 4
   582	%
   583	%c : C = D
   584	%f(c)
   585	\begin{Fortress}
   586	\(\KWD{trait} A\)\\
   587	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(c\COLONOP{}C) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
   588	\(\KWD{end}\)\\
   589	\(\KWD{trait} B \KWD{excludes} A \KWD{end}\)\\
   590	\(\KWD{trait} C \KWD{end}\)\\
   591	\(\KWD{object} D \KWD{extends} \{B,C\} \KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
   592	\(f(a\COLONOP{}A) = 3\)\\
   593	\(f(b\COLONOP{}B) = 4\)\\[4pt]
   594	\(c \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} C = D\)\\
   595	\(f(c)\)
   596	\end{Fortress}
   597	the call to \EXP{f(C)} resolves to the declaration
   598	%\EXP{f(a\COLONOP{}A)}
   599	\EXP{f(A)} despite the fact that the declaration
   600	%\EXP{f(b\COLONOP{}B)}
   601	\EXP{f(B)} is
   602	%dynamically directly
   603	applicable to the dynamic call \EXP{f(D)} and does not require
   604	coercion.
   605	
   606	
   607	
   608	
   609	\section{Restrictions on Coercion Declarations}
   610	\seclabel{restrictions-coercion}
   611	We place two restrictions on coercion declarations to ensure that it is
   612	always possible to resolve coercions.
   613	
   614	It is a static error for a type to define a coercion from any of its
   615	subtypes.  For example, the following program is statically rejected:
   616	%trait Number
   617	%  coerce(z:ZZ) = ...
   618	%end
   619	
   620	%trait ZZ extends Number end
   621	\begin{Fortress}
   622	\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Number}\)\\
   623	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(z\COLONOP\mathbb{Z}) = \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
   624	\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
   625	\(\KWD{trait} \mathbb{Z} \KWD{extends} \TYP{Number} \KWD{end}\)
   626	\end{Fortress}
   627	Instead, \VAR{z} of type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} can be coerced to type
   628	\TYP{Number} by
   629	%coerce_[\Number\](z)
   630	``\EXP{\mathrm{coerce}\llbracket\TYP{Number}\rrbracket(z)}''
   631	where \EXP{\mathrm{coerce}} is defined in \library\
   632	(as described in \secref{coercion-expr}).
   633	
   634	
   635	It is also a static error for cycles to exist in the type hierarchy
   636	produced by extension and coercion declarations.  Such cycles may be
   637	composed of solely subtype relationships or solely coercion or a
   638	mixture of the two.  In all cases the cycles are statically rejected.
   639	An example showing a cycle that is a mixture of subtype and coercion
   640	relationships follows:
   641	%trait A end
   642	
   643	%trait B extends A end
   644	
   645	%trait C extends B
   646	%  coerce(a:A) = ...
   647	%end
   648	\begin{Fortress}
   649	\(\KWD{trait} A \KWD{end} \)\\[4pt]
   650	\(\KWD{trait} B \KWD{extends} A \KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]

755	%fn x => coerce_[\D\](f(coerce_[\A\](x)))
   756	\begin{Fortress}
   757	\(\KWD{fn}\:x \Rightarrow \mathrm{coerce}\llbracket{}D\rrbracket(f(\mathrm{coerce}\llbracket{}A\rrbracket(x)))\)
   758	\end{Fortress}
   759	
   760	
   761	\section{Automatic Widening}
   762	\seclabel{widening}
   763	
   764	\begin{Grammar}
   765	\emph{Coercion} &::=&
   766	\KWD{coerce}\option{\emph{StaticParams}}\texttt(\emph{BindId} \emph{IsType}\texttt)\emph{CoercionClauses} \KWD{widens} \EXP{=} \emph{Expr}\\
   767	
   768	\end{Grammar}
   769	
   770	
   771	Fortress supports what is sometimes called ``widest-need'' evaluation
   772	of numerical expressions.  To see the problem, suppose that \VAR{a}
   773	and \VAR{b} are 32-bit floating-point numbers and \VAR{c} is a 64-bit
   774	floating-point number.  It is easy, and tempting, to write an
   775	expression such as
   776	%% c = c + a \cdot b
   777	\begin{Fortress}
   778	\(c = c + a \cdot b\)
   779	\end{Fortress}
   780	but if you stop to think about it, if interpreted naively it will
   781	compute the product \EXP{a \cdot b} as a 32-bit floating-point number,
   782	and the impression that the sum may be accurate to the precision of a
   783	64-bit floating-point number is only an illusion.  Widest-need
   784	processing takes context into account and ``widens'' (or ``upgrades'')
   785	the operands \VAR{a} and \VAR{b} to 64-bit floating-point numbers
   786	before the product is computed, so that the product will be computed
   787	as a 64-bit result.
   788	
   789	Before widening is considered, a Fortress compiler,
   790	in its normal course of operation, analyzes
   791	an expression bottom-up.  For every functional invocation, it needs
   792	to statically identify a specific declaration to be invoked.
   793	Once this is done, then for %every argument position of
   794	every functional invocation, one of two conditions holds:
   795	(a) The type of the argument expression is a subtype of the
   796	    type of the parameter in the identified declaration.
   797	(b) The type of the argument expression can be coerced to the
   798	    type of the parameter in the identified declaration.
   799	
   800	This process has to be done bottom-up because in order to select a
   801	specific declaration for a functional invocation, it is necessary to
   802	know the types of the argument expressions, and if an argument
   803	expression is itself a functional invocation, it is necessary to
   804	select the specific declaration for that invocation in order to find
   805	out the return type of the invocation.
   806	
   807	Once an expression has been fully analyzed in this way, then widening
   808	is performed as a top-down process.  For each functional invocation
   809	that appears in a context where a coercion can occur, ask
   810	whether the argument expression (which, remember, is a functional invocation)
   811	falls under case (a) or case (b) above.  If case (b), coercion of the
   812	functional result is required; if the relevant coercion declaration is
   813	a ``widening'' coercion, then this functional invocation is a
   814	candidate for widening.  Call the type of the functional invocation
   815	\VAR{T}, and call the expected type of the coercion context, \VAR{U}.
   816	
   817	
   818	When the functional call was considered during the bottom-up analysis,
   819	in general many overloaded declarations may have been considered; of
   820	all those that were applicable with coercion
   821	to the static call, the most specific one was chosen.
   822	When considering widening, we consider the same set of declarations, but
   823	first discard all declarations whose return types are not subtypes of
   824	\VAR{U}.  Then if any remain, and there is a unique most specific one
   825	among them, then that declaration is attached to the functional call
   826	instead.  In this way a coercion step is eliminated (coercion is no
   827	longer needed to convert the result of the functional invocation from
   828	type \VAR{T} to type \VAR{U}), possibly at the expense of requiring
   829	a new coercion in a subexpression---but this is exactly the desired
   830	effect.  Once this is done, then the subexpressions of the functional
   831	call are processed recursively.
   832	
   833	
   834	This process is general enough not only to provide for
   835	widening floating-point precision, but to handle two other cases
   836	of interest as well: widening point computations to interval computations,
   837	and widening computations involving aggregate data structures whose
   838	components are widenable.  For example, in \EXP{d (v \times w)} suppose that
   839	\VAR{d} is of type $\mathbb{R}64$ and \VAR{v} and \VAR{w} are 3-vectors with components
   840	of type $\mathbb{R}32$; this strategy is capable of promoting \VAR{v} and \VAR{w}
   841	to 3-vectors with components of type $\mathbb{R}64$ and then performing all
   842	computations with $\mathbb{R}64$ precision.
   843	
   844	Let's go through the example of \EXP{c + a \cdot b} in detail.
   845	The relevant declarations might look something like this:
   846	%trait RR32
   847	%  ...
   848	%end
   849	%
   850	%trait RR64
   851	%  coerce(x:RR32) widens = ...
   852	%  ...
   853	%end
   854	
   855	%opr DOT(l: RR32, r: RR32): RR32 = ... (* 1 *)
   856	%opr DOT(l: RR64, r: RR64): RR64 = ... (* 2 *)
   857	%opr +(l: RR32, r: RR32): RR32 = ... (* 3 *)
   858	%opr +(l: RR64, r: RR64): RR64 = ... (* 4 *)
   859	\begin{Fortress}
   860	\(\KWD{trait}\:\mathbb{R}32\)\\
   861	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
   862	\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
   863	\(\KWD{trait}\:\mathbb{R}64\)\\
   864	{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{coerce}(x\COLONOP\mathbb{R}32) \KWD{widens}\: = \ldots\)\\
   865	\(  \ldots\)\-\\\poptabs
   866	\(\KWD{end}\)\\[4pt]
   867	\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\cdot}(l\COLON \mathbb{R}32, r\COLON \mathbb{R}32)\COLON \mathbb{R}32 = \ldots \mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  1 \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
   868	\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\cdot}(l\COLON \mathbb{R}64, r\COLON \mathbb{R}64)\COLON \mathbb{R}64 = \ldots \mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  2 \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
   869	\(\KWD{opr} +(l\COLON \mathbb{R}32, r\COLON \mathbb{R}32)\COLON \mathbb{R}32 = \ldots \mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  3 \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
   870	\(\KWD{opr} +(l\COLON \mathbb{R}64, r\COLON \mathbb{R}64)\COLON \mathbb{R}64 = \ldots \mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  4 \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)
   871	\end{Fortress}
   872	
   873	The bottom-up analysis observes that \VAR{a} and \VAR{b} are both of type
   874	\EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, and discovers that declarations \EXP{1} and \EXP{2}
   875	are both applicable to the product, but declaration \EXP{1}
   876	would be chosen because it requires no coercion and declaration \EXP{2}
   877	would require coercion of both arguments to type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
   878	The analysis then observes that \VAR{c} has type \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
   879	and the product expression has type \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, so declaration
   880	\EXP{3} is not applicable but declaration \EXP{4} is applicable
   881	(though requiring a coercion from \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} to \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} for its second argument).
   882	
   883	Now the top-down widening analysis is performed.  The product is
   884	a functional call that is an argument to another functional call,
   885	and its result requires coercion, and that coercion is a widening
   886	coercion.  Therefore the compiler reconsiders the applicable
   887	declarations, which were declarations \EXP{1} and \EXP{2}.
   888	The result type of declaration \EXP{1} is not a subtype
   889	of \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, but the result type of declaration \EXP{2}
   890	is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} (in fact, it \emph{is} \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}).
   891	Declaration \EXP{2} is the most specific among the applicable declarations
   892	with that property (in fact, in this example it's the only one),
   893	so declaration \EXP{2} replaces declaration \EXP{1} for the
   894	product invocation.  This in turn requires \VAR{a} and \VAR{b}
   895	to be coerced from type \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} to \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}
   896	before the product is performed.
   897	
   898	Widening is a tricky business, best left to expert library designers.
   899	When used judiciously, it can greatly improve the precision of
   900	numerical computations without requiring a great deal of thought on
   901	the part of the application programmer and without cluttering up code
   902	with explicit conversions.
   903	
   904	
   905	\emph{Future versions of this specification will include tables of
   906	  coercions and widening coercions supported by \library.}

95	And a reference to where that is done should be appear in this section (probably at the beginning of the section).
    96	}
    97	
    98	\note{Ought we discuss digit-group separators here?
    99	Or is that just part of lexical structure?
   100	(I think we intend that a numeral consisting of digits and digit-group separators has
   101	type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeral}\llbracket{}n,10,v\rrbracket}
   102	for appropriate values of \VAR{n} and \VAR{v}.)}
   103	
   104	A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the number of
   105	digits) then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$ be the
   106	radix) has type \EXP{\TYP{NaturalNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,r,v\rrbracket}
   107	where $v$ is
   108	the value of the $n$-digit numeral interpreted in radix $r$.
   109	
   110	A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
   111	of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
   112	the radix point) has type
   113	\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is
   114	the value of the numeral, with the radix point deleted,
   115	interpreted in radix ten.
   116	
   117	A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
   118	of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
   119	the radix point), then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$
   120	be the radix) has the following type:
   121	\begin{Fortress}
   122	\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
   123	\end{Fortress}
   124	where $v$ is the value of the $n$-digit numeral, with the radix point
   125	deleted, interpreted in radix $r$.
   126	
   127	Every numeral also has type
   128	\EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
   129	for appropriate values of \VAR{n}, \VAR{m}, \VAR{r}, and \VAR{v}.
   130	
   131	
   132	Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types
   133	because, as in common mathematical usage,
   134	we expect them to be polymorphic.
   135	For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
   136	converting it immediately to a floating-point number
   137	may lose precision.
   138	If that numeral is used in an expression
   139	involving floating-point intervals,
   140	it would be better to convert it directly to an interval.
   141	Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
   142	This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
   143	interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
   144	(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
   145	in Fortress).
   146	\Library\ define coercions
   147	from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
   148	and rational numbers (for compound numerals).
   149	
   150	
   151	\marginnote{What is an ``integer'' in this context?}
   152	In Fortress, dividing two integers using the $/$ operator produces
   153	a \emph{rational number};\marginnote{Not if the second integer is 0.}
   154	this is true regardless of whether
   155	the integers are of type $\mathbb{Z}$ (or \txt{ZZ}),
   156	$\mathbb{Z}64$ (or \txt{ZZ64}), $\mathbb{N}32$ (or \txt{NN32}), or
   157	whatever.  Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of rationals
   158	are always exact; thus values such as \EXP{1/3} are represented exactly in
   159	Fortress.
   160	
   161	\note{We should give an example with a radix specifier.}
   162	Numerals containing a radix point are actually rational
   163	literals; thus \EXP{3.125} has the rational value \EXP{3125/1000}.
   164	The quotient of two integer literals is a static expression
   165	(described in \secref{static-expr}) whose value is rational.
   166	Similarly, a sequence of digits with a radix point followed by the symbol
   167	$\times$ and an integer literal raised to an integer literal,
   168	such as \EXP{6.0221415 \times 10^{23}}
   169	is a static expression whose value is rational.
   170	If such static expressions are mentioned as part of a floating-point
   171	computation, the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then
   172	converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring
   173	at most one floating-point rounding error.
   174	But in general rational computations may also be performed at run time,
   175	not just at compile time.
   176	\note{This specifies too much about the implementation:
   177	I don't think we should mention a compiler at all, except perhaps as informal discussion.
   178	In particular, wouldn't it be correct if this arithmetic were actually deferred and
   179	performed exactly at run time?}
   180	
   181	
   182	A rational number can be thought of as a pair of integers $p$ and $q$
   183	that have been reduced to ``standard form in lowest terms'';
   184	that is, $q > 0$ and there is no nonzero integer $k$
   185	such that $p \over k$ and $q \over k$ are integers
   186	and $\left| {p \over k} \right| + \left| {q \over k} \right|
   187		< \left| p \right| + \left| q \right|$.
   188	The type $\mathbb{Q}$ includes all such rational numbers.
   189	
   190	The type $\mathbb{Q}^*$ relaxes the requirement $q>0$ to $q \geq 0$ and
   191	includes two extra values, \EXP{1/0} and \EXP{-1/0} (sometimes called ``the
   192	infinite rational'' and ``the indefinite rational'').
   193	\marginnote{Is there any subtyping or coercion relationship between \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and
   194	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}?
   195	If \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}
   196	then static checking would normally disallow the assignment,
   197	so is this a relaxation to that rule?  If so, the static checker needs to know about it.}
   198	If a value of type $\mathbb{Q}^*$ is assigned to a
   199	variable of type $\mathbb{Q}$, a \TYP{DivisionByZero} is thrown
   200	at run time if the value is \EXP{1/0} or \EXP{-1/0}.
   201	The type \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}} includes all of \EXP{1/0}, \EXP{-1/0}, and
   202	\EXP{0/0}.
   203	The advantage of $\mathbb{Q}^{\#}$ is that it is closed under the rational
   204	operations $+$, $-$, $\times$, and $/$.
   205	In ASCII, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*}, and
   206	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}^\#} are written as \txt{QQ}, \txt{QQ\_star}, and
   207	\txt{QQ\_splat}, respectively.
   208	See \secref{advanced-rationals} for definitions of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*},
   209	and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^\#}.
   210	
   211	
   212	
   213	\subsection{Pi}
   214	\seclabel{pi}
   215	
   216	The object named \EXP{\pi} (or \txt{pi}) may be used to represent the ratio
   217	of the circumference of a circle to its diameter rather than a specific
   218	floating-point value or interval value.
   219	In Fortress, \EXP{\pi} has type
   220	\EXP{\TYP{RationalValueTimesPi}\llbracket\VAR{false},1,1\rrbracket}.
   221	When used in a floating-point computation, it becomes
   222	a floating-point value of the appropriate precision; when used in an interval
   223	computation, it becomes an interval of the appropriate precision.
   224	
   225	\subsection{Infinity and Zero}
   226	
   227	The object named \EXP{\infty} has type \EXP{\TYP{ExtendedIntegerValue}\llbracket\VAR{true},0,\VAR{true}\rrbracket}.
   228	One can negate \EXP{\infty} to get a negative infinity.
   229	
   230	\note{What about spaces?  That is, is ``- 0'' treated the same as ``-0'', for example?}
